claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-derived alloys are controlled by a magnetically mediated phase transformation.
Reducing or eliminating Mn reduces magnetic frustration.
CrCoNi undergoes a deformation-triggered FCC-to-HCP transformation associated with dislocation slip.
The FCC-to-HCP transformation enhances strength through transformation-induced plasticity.
The FCC-to-HCP transformation enhances work hardening.
The Mn-containing equiatomic quinary alloy suppresses the deformation-induced FCC-to-HCP transformation and consequently has lower strengthening than CrCoNi.
The investigated quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys can all be prepared as single-phase FCC structures by thermomechanical processing.
A controlled investigation should vary Mn content across quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys and then subject them to tensile deformation and microstructural characterization.
Room-temperature tensile testing combined with TEM, EBSD, XRD, and magnetic measurements can test the proposed relationship.
Absence of Mn-driven magnetic frustration lowers the energetic barrier for deformation-induced HCP martensite formation.
The HCP transformation nucleates at dislocation slip sites or their interactions with internal boundaries.
Transformation-generated HCP regions introduce additional barriers to dislocation motion.
Mn magnetic frustration stabilizes the FCC state and suppresses the FCC-to-HCP transformation.
Relative to equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi, CrCoNi should retain greater strength without sacrificing plastic deformation.
Mn-depleted quaternary and ternary alloys will develop a higher post-deformation HCP phase fraction than equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi.
Mn-depleted alloys will have higher yield strength and work-hardening rates than equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi.
The hypothesis is limited to initially single-phase FCC alloys in which deformation-induced transformation is possible.
Pre-existing BCC phases or microstructural evolution such as coarsening can mask the proposed transformation effect.
Failure of Mn-depleted alloys to show both increased deformation-induced HCP fraction and enhanced strength and work hardening relative to the quinary control would falsify the mechanism.
